title: Episode 42: Accessing Workshop Materials
description: Downloading the repository, reading offline, keeping updated, audio format.
concepts: How to clone or download the workshop repository
Reading materials in markdown versus HTML format
Using the HTML site at community-access.org
Reading offline: cloning and opening in VS Code or a text editor
Keeping your copy updated: git pull
The podcast audio series as an alternative format
Printing or exporting materials for reference
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're focusing on a very practical question: how do you actually access these workshop materials, read them in the format that works best for you, download them, and keep your copy current over time?

[JAMIE]
I like that this is practical, because learners may be wondering, is there one official way to read all this?

[ALEX]
No, and that's the point. The materials are available in multiple formats. There are Markdown source files, pre-built HTML pages, and, when enabled by the facilitator, a live GitHub Pages website. This appendix exists to explain how to use each option, including offline access and updates.

[JAMIE]
And we should mention the administrative context too, right?

[ALEX]
Exactly. There is an audio companion episode for this material, this appendix is a reference companion to the pre-workshop setup chapter, and the authoritative source for the materials is the Community-Access GitHub repository for Git Going with GitHub.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Before we walk through the options, here are some quick access tips tailored to different users.

[JAMIE]
Let's start with screen reader users.

[ALEX]
If you're using a screen reader, the GitHub Pages site includes skip-to-content links and ARIA landmarks. On those pages, you can press D in NVDA or R in JAWS to move to the main landmark. On GitHub.com, if you're on the repository main page, press T to open the file finder so you can type a filename and jump straight to it without working through the full file tree. And after cloning the repository, opening it in VS Code gives you the Explorer panel with Control+Shift+E, where you can browse the tree with arrow keys.

[JAMIE]
What about low vision learners?

[ALEX]
The HTML version in the html folder usually provides the most polished reading experience. It's styled, navigable, and works offline in a browser. If you're reading Markdown source files, VS Code's built-in preview with Control+Shift+V can render headings, links, and code blocks in a cleaner way than raw text alone. And if you're downloading a ZIP from GitHub, remember that the Code button is the green button near the top of the repository page.

[JAMIE]
And for sighted users more generally?

[ALEX]
There are three main access paths: the GitHub Pages site, which is online and styled; GitHub.com, where Markdown is rendered in the browser; and a local clone, which works offline and is editable. The docs folder holds the Markdown source, the html folder holds pre-built HTML, and cloning with Git gives you a full copy that you can later update with git pull. A ZIP download is just a snapshot and does not update by itself.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
A simple way to think about the flow is this: you can browse online, read on GitHub.com, download everything, download just one file, learn what each folder contains, read offline, update your local copy, and then decide which format best matches your needs.

[JAMIE]
So let's take those one at a time. Suppose I just want to browse online in the easiest possible way.

[ALEX]
If the facilitator has enabled GitHub Pages for the repository, the workshop materials may be available as a website at a GitHub Pages URL, something like an organization dot github dot io address followed by the site name. Your facilitator should provide the exact URL.

[JAMIE]
And once I have it?

[ALEX]
Open it in your browser. The landing page, usually index dot html, functions as the workshop homepage and is effectively the website counterpart to the README. From there, you can navigate within a page by headings, using the H key in browse mode for NVDA or JAWS. Internal links between chapters and appendices should work, so cross-references take you directly where you need to go. And it's worth bookmarking that URL so you can get back to it quickly during the workshop.

[JAMIE]
This sounds especially good for accessibility.

[ALEX]
Yes. The HTML pages include skip links, breadcrumb navigation, and ARIA landmarks. So for screen reader users, jumping to the main landmark with D in NVDA or R in JAWS can make navigation much faster. And if you want the deeper technical background on how GitHub Pages publishing works, there's a separate appendix dedicated to GitHub Pages.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let's say I don't want a separate website. I just want to read directly on GitHub.com.

[ALEX]
You can do that too. Go to the repository page your facilitator shares. On GitHub.com, the README renders automatically on the main repository page, so you begin with a formatted overview. Then click into the docs folder to find all the chapters and appendices. When you open any Markdown file ending in dot md, GitHub renders it as formatted text with headings, links, and code blocks.

[JAMIE]
That sounds straightforward visually, but what about screen reader navigation inside the repository?

[ALEX]
A few important details. The repository file listing behaves like a grid or table. You can use T to jump to the file table, then move through rows with arrow keys. Once you're inside a file, GitHub renders the Markdown, so heading navigation with H works well. At the top of a file view, breadcrumb links show the path, for example repository, then docs, then a specific file. Those breadcrumbs help you move back up a level. And again, on the repository main page, T opens the Go to File finder so you can type the filename directly.

[JAMIE]
That's one of those shortcuts that can save a lot of effort.

[ALEX]
Absolutely.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What if I want everything on my own machine?

[ALEX]
Then you're in the downloading section, and there are two main approaches. Option A is cloning with Git, which is the recommended method. Option B is downloading a ZIP if you don't want to use Git.

[JAMIE]
Let's do the Git option first.

[ALEX]
Cloning gives you a full copy of the repository and lets you update later with git pull. The commands are straightforward: first run git clone with the repository URL, then change into the folder with cd Learning-Room.

[JAMIE]
And after that, what do I actually have?

[ALEX]
You have the whole repository on your computer: Markdown source, HTML output, scripts, and learning-room materials. If you're using a screen reader, it's a good moment to open the folder in VS Code, for example with code dot, then use Control+Shift+E for the Explorer panel. From there, arrow through files and press Enter to open one in the editor.

[JAMIE]
So clone is best if I want a living copy, not just a one-time download.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[JAMIE]
Now the no-Git route: ZIP download.

[ALEX]
If Git isn't installed, or you simply prefer not to use the command line, go to the repository page on GitHub.com. Find the green Code button near the top of the file listing. Activate it to open the dropdown menu, then choose Download ZIP. Save the file and extract it on your computer.

[JAMIE]
And for screen reader users, that Code button can be annoying to find if you don't know where it lives.

[ALEX]
Right, so the appendix gives very specific guidance. The Code button is near the repository description and after the branch selector. In NVDA or JAWS browse mode, press B to jump between buttons until you hear Code. Activate it with Enter or Space. Then arrow down in the dropdown until you reach Download ZIP.

[JAMIE]
Important caveat?

[ALEX]
A ZIP download is a snapshot. It does not update automatically. If the repository changes, your ZIP copy does not know that. You'll need to download a fresh ZIP later if you want a newer version.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Sometimes people don't need everything. What if I only want one chapter or one cheat sheet?

[ALEX]
Then download an individual file. From GitHub.com, navigate to the file, activate the Raw button above the file content, and the browser will show the raw text of the file. Then save it with Control+S on Windows or Linux, or Command+S on macOS.

[JAMIE]
And if it's an HTML file instead of Markdown?

[ALEX]
Go to the html folder, find the corresponding dot html file, and use the same Raw then Save approach.

[JAMIE]
What if I've already cloned the repository?

[ALEX]
Then you already have every file locally. Just open the folder and copy out the specific files you need.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's talk about folder structure, because that can be confusing when learners first open a repository.

[ALEX]
Definitely. The docs folder contains all 17 numbered chapters, from 00 through 16, plus 31 appendices labeled A through Z and then AA through AE. Those are Markdown files.

[JAMIE]
So docs is the source reading material in Markdown.

[ALEX]
Correct. The html folder contains pre-built HTML versions of every Markdown file. Within that, html slash docs contains HTML versions of all chapters and appendices specifically. The learning-room folder contains practice repository files, challenges, group exercises, and setup guides, again mainly in Markdown. The html slash learning-room folder contains HTML versions of those learning-room documents.

[JAMIE]
And then there are the project-maintenance folders.

[ALEX]
Yes. The dot github folder includes issue templates, a pull request template, Copilot agents, and slash commands, usually in YAML and Markdown. The scripts folder contains the build script that converts Markdown to HTML, using JavaScript. And the repository root contains items like the README, agendas, facilitator guide, contributing guide, and other project files.

[JAMIE]
That's useful, because it tells learners not just where to read, but where different kinds of work happen.

[ALEX]
Exactly right.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now suppose I'm offline. Can I still use all this effectively?

[ALEX]
Yes. Once you've downloaded or cloned the repository, you can read everything offline.

[JAMIE]
Let's separate Markdown and HTML.

[ALEX]
For Markdown files, open the dot md files in any text editor. They are plain text with lightweight markup. In VS Code, Control+Shift+V opens a rendered Markdown preview, which many learners find easier to read than raw syntax.

[JAMIE]
And the HTML path?

[ALEX]
Open html slash index dot html in any web browser. From there, internal links between pages should work locally, so you can move through the material without internet access. You can navigate among chapters using the links on the pages themselves, including bottom navigation.

[JAMIE]
Accessibility still works offline?

[ALEX]
Yes. The HTML files work offline the same way they do online. The ARIA landmarks, heading structure, and skip links are built into each file.

[JAMIE]
If someone asks for the best offline setup, what would you recommend?

[ALEX]
Two strong options. One is VS Code with the Markdown files: open the repository folder, browse with the Explorer, and read source files directly, using the preview when needed. The other is a browser with the local HTML site: open html slash index dot html and navigate from there. That gives the most polished reading experience.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Okay, now the maintenance question. How do I keep my copy updated?

[ALEX]
If you cloned with Git, navigate to your local copy, typically with cd Learning-Room, and run git pull.

[JAMIE]
And if I haven't changed anything locally, that should just update cleanly?

[ALEX]
Yes. If you have not made local changes, git pull should update your copy cleanly. If you have made local edits, Git will attempt to merge those changes with the incoming updates. And if that creates conflicts, you'll need merge conflict skills from the chapter on merge conflicts.

[JAMIE]
There's also one more step mentioned here after pulling.

[ALEX]
Right. After pulling, rebuild the HTML so your local generated site matches the latest Markdown source. The command given is npm run build:html.

[JAMIE]
And if I used a ZIP instead of a clone?

[ALEX]
Then there is no incremental update mechanism. You simply download a fresh ZIP from the repository and replace your local copy.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
This brings us to the big decision question: which format should I use?

[ALEX]
If you're reading during the workshop, GitHub Pages, meaning the online HTML site, is usually the best choice. It requires no setup, stays current, and is designed to be fully accessible.

[JAMIE]
For offline reference?

[ALEX]
Local HTML from the html folder. It works in any browser, doesn't require internet, and gives you the styled reading experience.

[JAMIE]
For editing and contributing?

[ALEX]
Use the Markdown source files in docs. Those are the canonical source files you edit, and then the HTML is rebuilt from them.

[JAMIE]
For a quick lookup of one section while I'm already in a browser?

[ALEX]
GitHub.com is great for that. You can jump straight to a file without downloading everything.

[JAMIE]
For archiving a copy?

[ALEX]
Either a ZIP download or a Git clone gives you a full snapshot. But for staying updated long-term, a Git clone is better because you can use one command, git pull.

[JAMIE]
Let's revisit the learning-card guidance by audience, because it's full of useful detail.

[ALEX]
For screen reader users, the GitHub Pages HTML site is usually the most accessible choice during the workshop because every page includes skip links, landmarks, and consistent heading structure. For offline reference, the local HTML files in the html folder work essentially the same way. For contributing edits, work in the Markdown source in docs using VS Code, because that's the canonical source that generates everything else.

[JAMIE]
And low vision guidance?

[ALEX]
GitHub Pages and local HTML both support browser zoom to 200 percent or more without layout breakage, so choose whichever gives you the better reading experience. VS Code's Markdown preview inherits your editor theme, which is helpful if you use a high-contrast theme. And if you're reading on GitHub.com, GitHub's dark theme can reduce eye strain during long sessions.

[JAMIE]
And for sighted users broadly?

[ALEX]
Use the GitHub Pages site during the workshop for the cleanest hyperlinked reading experience with no setup. Clone the repository if you want a permanent offline copy, and remember that html slash index dot html acts as a local homepage. And if you want to improve the materials, edit the Markdown in docs; those changes are what get rebuilt into HTML, typically through the project's build process and automation.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we wrap up, I want to make sure we keep the source-of-truth piece in view. Where should learners verify current facts if GitHub changes something?

[ALEX]
Use the official references: GitHub Docs and the GitHub Changelog. Those are the authoritative external sources listed for this appendix. The appendix also provides a section-level source map, pointing each major part of this topic back to those official references.

[JAMIE]
So the practical takeaway is: choose the format that matches your goal.

[ALEX]
Exactly. If you want easiest reading during the workshop, use GitHub Pages. If you want quick browser access, use GitHub.com. If you want a full offline, updateable copy, clone the repository. If you want a one-time snapshot with no Git required, download a ZIP. And if you're contributing, edit the Markdown source.

[JAMIE]
That's a helpful framework, especially for learners who may have assumed there was only one correct way to access the materials.

[ALEX]
There isn't one single correct way. There is a best-fit way for your task, your device, and your accessibility needs.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
And from here, learners can continue on to the appendix about GitHub Skills, revisit the resources appendix, or return to the pre-workshop setup material that this appendix supports.

[JAMIE]
See you next time.

# Appendix Y: Accessing and Downloading Workshop Materials
>
> **Listen to Episode 42:** [Accessing Workshop Materials](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

> **Reference companion to:** [Chapter 00: Pre-Workshop Setup](00-pre-workshop-setup.md)
>
> **Authoritative source:** [Community-Access/git-going-with-github](https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github)

## How to Get, Read, and Keep These Documents

> **Why this appendix exists:** The workshop content is available in multiple formats - Markdown source files, pre-built HTML pages, and a live GitHub Pages site. This guide explains how to access each format, download materials for offline use, and keep your copy up to date.

### Learning Cards: Accessing Workshop Materials

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- The GitHub Pages site includes skip-to-content links and ARIA landmarks -- press `D` (NVDA) or `R` (JAWS) to jump to the main content landmark on any page
- On GitHub.com, press `T` on the repository's main page to open the file finder -- type any filename to jump directly to it without navigating the file tree
- After cloning the repository, open it in VS Code and use the Explorer panel (`Ctrl+Shift+E`) to browse the file tree with arrow keys

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- The HTML version in the `html/` folder provides the most polished reading experience with styled, navigable pages that work offline in any browser
- For reading Markdown source files, use VS Code's built-in preview (`Ctrl+Shift+V`) which renders headings, links, and code blocks in a formatted view
- When downloading a ZIP from GitHub, the Code button and its dropdown appear near the top of the repository page -- look for the green button

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- Three ways to access materials: GitHub Pages site (online, styled), GitHub.com (browse rendered Markdown), or local clone (offline, editable)
- The repository's `docs/` folder contains all Markdown source files; the `html/` folder contains pre-built HTML versions of every page
- Use `git clone` for a full copy you can update with `git pull` -- ZIP downloads are snapshots that do not update automatically

</details>

## Table of Contents

1. [Browsing Online (GitHub Pages)](#1-browsing-online-github-pages)
2. [Reading on GitHub.com](#2-reading-on-githubcom)
3. [Downloading Everything](#3-downloading-everything)
4. [Downloading Individual Files](#4-downloading-individual-files)
5. [What's in Each Folder](#5-whats-in-each-folder)
6. [Offline Reading](#6-offline-reading)
7. [Keeping Your Copy Updated](#7-keeping-your-copy-updated)
8. [Which Format Should I Use?](#8-which-format-should-i-use)

## 1. Browsing Online (GitHub Pages)

If the facilitator has enabled GitHub Pages for this repository, the workshop materials are available as a website at a URL like:

```text
https://<organization>.github.io/Learning-Room/
```

Your facilitator will share the exact URL. Once you have it:

1. Open the URL in your browser
2. The landing page (`index.html`) is the workshop homepage - equivalent to the README
3. Use headings (`H` key in NVDA/JAWS browse mode) to navigate within any page
4. All internal links between chapters and appendices work - click any cross-reference to go directly to that page
5. Bookmark the URL for quick access during the workshop

**Screen reader tip:** The HTML pages include skip-to-content links, breadcrumb navigation, and ARIA landmarks. Press `D` (NVDA) or `R` (JAWS) to jump to the main landmark on any page.

For details on how GitHub Pages works, see [Appendix P - Publishing with GitHub Pages](appendix-w-github-pages.md).

## 2. Reading on GitHub.com

You can read every file directly on GitHub.com without downloading anything:

1. Go to the repository page (your facilitator will share the link)
2. The README renders automatically as the repository homepage
3. Click into the `docs/` folder to see all chapters and appendices
4. Click any `.md` file - GitHub renders it as formatted text with headings, links, and code blocks

### Navigating the repository with a screen reader

- **File list:** The repository file listing is a grid. Use `T` to jump to the file table, then arrow keys to navigate rows
- **File content:** Once inside a file, GitHub renders the Markdown. Use `H` to navigate headings
- **Breadcrumbs:** At the top of each file view, breadcrumb links show the path (e.g., `Learning-Room / docs / 06-working-with-pull-requests.md`). Use these to navigate back
- **Go to File shortcut:** Press `T` on the repository's main page to open the file finder - type any filename to jump to it

## 3. Downloading Everything

### Option A: Clone with Git (recommended)

Cloning gives you a full copy of the repository that you can update later with `git pull`:

```bash
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/community-access/git-going-with-github.git

# Move into the folder
cd Learning-Room
```

After cloning, every file (Markdown source, HTML output, scripts, learning-room materials) is on your computer.

**Screen reader tip:** After cloning, open the folder in VS Code (`code .`) and use the Explorer panel (`Ctrl+Shift+E`) to browse the file tree. Press `Enter` on any file to open it in the editor.

### Option B: Download ZIP (no Git required)

If you do not have Git installed or prefer not to use the command line:

1. Go to the repository page on GitHub.com
2. Press `T` to find the file finder, or navigate to the green **Code** button (it is a dropdown button near the top of the file listing)
3. Activate the **Code** button - a dropdown menu opens
4. Choose **Download ZIP**
5. Save the file and extract it to a folder on your computer

#### Screen reader navigation for the Code dropdown

- The **Code** button is near the repository description, after the branch selector
- In NVDA/JAWS browse mode, press `B` to jump between buttons until you reach "Code"
- Activate it with `Enter` or `Space`
- The dropdown contains options including "Download ZIP" - arrow down to find it

**Note:** A ZIP download is a snapshot. It does not update automatically - see [Section 7](#7-keeping-your-copy-updated) for how to get updates.

## 4. Downloading Individual Files

To download a single file (for example, one chapter or the screen reader cheat sheet):

### From GitHub.com

1. Navigate to the file in the repository
2. Click the **Raw** button (it appears above the file content, in the toolbar with "Preview", "Code", "Blame" buttons)
3. The browser shows the raw file content
4. Press `Ctrl+S` (Windows/Linux) or `Cmd+S` (macOS) to save the page

**For HTML files:** Navigate to the `html/` folder and download the `.html` version of any file using the same Raw → Save method.

### From a cloned repository

If you have already cloned the repo, every file is already on your computer. Open the folder and copy whichever files you need.

## 5. What's in Each Folder

| Folder | Contents | Format |
| --------  | ----------  | --------  |
| `docs/` | All 17 chapters (00-16) and 31 appendices (A-Z, AA-AE) | Markdown (`.md`) |
| `html/` | Pre-built HTML versions of every Markdown file | HTML (`.html`) |
| `html/docs/` | HTML versions of all chapters and appendices | HTML (`.html`) |
| `learning-room/` | Practice repository files: challenges, group exercises, setup guides | Markdown (`.md`) |
| `html/learning-room/` | HTML versions of learning-room documents | HTML (`.html`) |
| `.github/` | Issue templates, PR template, Copilot agents, slash commands | YAML and Markdown |
| `scripts/` | Build script that converts Markdown to HTML | JavaScript |
| Root (`/`) | README, agendas, facilitator guide, contributing guide, and other project files | Markdown (`.md`) |

## 6. Offline Reading

Once you have downloaded or cloned the repository, you can read everything offline:

### Reading Markdown files

Open `.md` files in any text editor. They are plain text with lightweight formatting syntax. VS Code renders Markdown with a preview panel (`Ctrl+Shift+V`).

### Reading HTML files

1. Open `html/index.html` in any web browser
2. All internal links between pages work locally - no internet connection required
3. Navigate between chapters using the links at the bottom of each page

**Screen reader tip:** The HTML files work the same offline as online. All ARIA landmarks, heading structure, and skip links are embedded in each file.

### Recommended offline reading setup

- **VS Code with Markdown:** Open the repo folder in VS Code, browse the Explorer, and read files directly in the editor. Use `Ctrl+Shift+V` to open the rendered preview
- **Browser with HTML:** Open `html/index.html` and navigate from there - this gives the most polished reading experience

## 7. Keeping Your Copy Updated

### If you cloned with Git

```bash
# Navigate to your local copy
cd Learning-Room

# Pull the latest changes
git pull
```

If you have not made local changes, this updates your copy cleanly. If you have local edits, Git will attempt to merge - see [Chapter 7 - Merge Conflicts](07-merge-conflicts.md) if needed.

After pulling, rebuild the HTML to ensure it matches:

```bash
npm run build:html
```

### If you downloaded a ZIP

Download a fresh ZIP from the repository and replace your local copy. There is no incremental update for ZIP downloads.

## 8. Which Format Should I Use?

| Need | Best format | Why |
| ------  | -------------  | -----  |
| Reading during the workshop | **GitHub Pages** (online HTML) | No setup, always current, fully accessible |
| Offline reference | **Local HTML** (`html/` folder) | Works in any browser, no internet needed, styled and navigable |
| Editing or contributing | **Markdown** (`.md` files) | The source format - edit these, then rebuild HTML |
| Quick lookup of one section | **GitHub.com** | Navigate directly in the browser, no download |
| Archiving a copy | **ZIP download** or **Git clone** | Full snapshot of all materials |
| Staying updated long-term | **Git clone** | One-command updates with `git pull` |

### Learning Cards: Choosing the Right Format

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- For workshop use, the GitHub Pages HTML site is the most accessible option -- it includes skip links, landmarks, and proper heading structure in every page
- For offline reference, the local HTML files in the `html/` folder work identically to the online version with full navigation between pages
- For contributing edits, work with the Markdown source files in `docs/` using VS Code -- these are the canonical source that generates everything else

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- GitHub Pages and local HTML both support browser zoom to 200%+ without layout breakage -- use whichever gives you a better reading experience
- VS Code's Markdown preview inherits your editor theme -- if you use a high-contrast theme, the preview will match
- If viewing on GitHub.com, enable GitHub's dark theme (Settings then Appearance) for reduced eye strain during long reading sessions

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- Use the GitHub Pages site during the workshop for the most polished, hyperlinked reading experience with no setup required
- Clone the repository for a permanent offline copy -- the `html/index.html` file serves as a local homepage linking to all content
- The Markdown source in `docs/` is what you edit to contribute improvements -- changes are rebuilt to HTML automatically via the GitHub Actions workflow

</details>

---

*Next: [Appendix Z: GitHub Skills](appendix-z-github-skills.md)*  
*Back: [Appendix X: Resources](appendix-x-resources.md)*  
*Teaching chapter: [Chapter 00: Pre-Workshop Setup](00-pre-workshop-setup.md)*

## Authoritative Sources

Use these official references when you need the current source of truth for facts in this chapter.

- [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en)
- [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/)

### Section-Level Source Map

Use this map to verify facts for each major section in this file.

- **How to Get, Read, and Keep These Documents:** [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en), [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/)
- **1. Browsing Online (GitHub Pages):** [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en), [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/), [About Git](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-git/about-git), [GitHub flow](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-github/github-flow), [About pull requests](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/proposing-changes-to-your-work-with-pull-requests/about-pull-requests)
- **2. Reading on GitHub.com:** [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en), [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/), [About Git](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-git/about-git), [GitHub flow](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-github/github-flow), [About pull requests](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/proposing-changes-to-your-work-with-pull-requests/about-pull-requests)
- **3. Downloading Everything:** [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en), [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/)
- **4. Downloading Individual Files:** [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en), [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/)
- **5. What's in Each Folder:** [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en), [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/)
- **6. Offline Reading:** [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en), [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/)
- **7. Keeping Your Copy Updated:** [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en), [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/)
- **8. Which Format Should I Use?:** [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en), [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/)

currentFacts: The Accessibility Agents collection grows over time. Refer to it as a living catalog rather than asserting a fixed count of agents.
Challenge 15 (Discover Accessibility Agents) is browse-first. Learners are not required to fork the accessibility-agents repository to complete it.
Completing Challenge 15 unlocks Challenge 16 (Capstone Project) plus Bonus Challenges A through E. The bonus challenges are a structured unlock path, not "things to do if you finish early".

Challenge 16 is titled "Capstone Project". It accepts contributions to Accessibility Agents, GLOW, or any other meaningful repository. Review-ready drafts and contribution plans are valid evidence of completion.
The Learning Room repository is where Day 1 contributions happen (issue, branch, commit, pull request, merge). It is provisioned per learner.
Hosts are Alex (warm expert) and Jamie (curious co-host who asks the questions learners hesitate to ask). They are colleagues, not teacher and student.

[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're working with one of those GitHub features that quietly makes open source collaboration much easier: issue templates.

[JAMIE]
And this is a great one for people who have ever opened a blank issue form and thought, what exactly am I supposed to put here?

[ALEX]
Exactly. An issue template turns that blank box into a guided experience. Instead of guessing what maintainers need, contributors get prompts, structure, and clear required fields. That reduces back-and-forth, improves quality, and helps teams act on issues faster.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just about formatting. It's about making contributions clearer and more usable.

[ALEX]
Yes, and especially in accessibility work. If someone is reporting an accessibility barrier, a vague report can be hard to reproduce. A thoughtful template can ask where the problem occurred, what assistive technology was involved, what the expected behavior was, and how severe the barrier is.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we get into the design challenge, what should learners already have in place?

[ALEX]
A few practical things. First, you should already know how to work with GitHub issues at a basic level. Second, you need a repository where you can create or edit files, usually your fork or your own repo. Third, it really helps to use an editor with YAML syntax highlighting, such as VS Code.

[JAMIE]
And some things are recommended but not strictly required, right?

[ALEX]
Right. Familiarity with GitHub Copilot can help if you want to generate variations, but it's optional. Basic terminal comfort is useful, though you can also use the GitHub web editor or github.dev. And if you already filled out the workshop registration template earlier in this course, that template becomes a learning example now.

[JAMIE]
I like that. You've already used a professional issue template, so now you reverse-engineer it.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Also, there's an administrative note here: this chapter is meant to prepare you for a later workflow using a template-building agent. The advice is to complete the manual template chapter first, then use the automation later.

[JAMIE]
And time-wise?

[ALEX]
Plan roughly two to two and a half hours if you do the exercises and some YAML troubleshooting.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The learning pattern for this challenge is analyze, remix, create, and test.

[JAMIE]
That feels approachable. First understand an existing template, then adapt one, then optionally build another version from scratch, then verify it works.

[ALEX]
That's the idea. The workshop recommendation frames Challenge 14 as design-focused rather than automation-focused. You're producing evidence of understanding, often as an issue comment or a pull request, rather than trying to satisfy a complicated code runtime.

[JAMIE]
Though there is still one small autograded requirement in the challenge template itself.

[ALEX]
Yes. For the assigned challenge issue, the autograder checks that a YAML file exists in the repository
